extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date. CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse. The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses. Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives. “The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.” Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta. “We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said. Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention … One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says. The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions. Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see. Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done. It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.” Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop. “You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.” Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline. Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf. Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping. Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal. The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion. Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.” Anthropic releases Opus 5.5 with lower prices and Fable-level performance Russell Brandom Meta’s Muse is outpacing ChatGPT’s early mobile launch Sarah Perez Tilly Norwood’s press tour is going about as well as you’d expect for an AI Amanda Silberling Anthropic is operating a lab that conducts biology experiments Julie Bort A new kind of AI model from a ChatGPT inventor is thrilling developers Tim Fernholz OpenAI caught its models leaving notes to successors to hide bad behavior Rebecca Bellan Microsoft exec called AI scraping ‘the largest theft of labor in human history,’ new unredacted filings reveal Rebecca Bellan

Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark , Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”
Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.
“We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said.
Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention …

One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says.

The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions.

Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line , the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see.
Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.
It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.”

Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac , and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.

“You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.”

Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.
Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf.
Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.

The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion.

Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI agent fuels chip stock rally as AMD hits $1 trillion market cap - Crypto Briefing
passages: Meta ’s personal AI agent, Muse, has done something unusual for a software launch: it moved the entire semiconductor sector.

AMD crossed the $1 trillion market cap threshold for the first time, Intel surged roughly 12%, and Arm Holdings popped about 17%, all on the back of what is essentially a very smart digital assistant that can book your flights and fill out forms.
Meta is also exploring commerce opportunities tied to Muse.
AMD’s 10% jump to a $1 trillion valuation is particularly notable.
The company has been chasing that milestone while competing against Nvidia in the data center GPU market.
Ironically, it was a CPU-heavy workload that finally pushed it over the line.
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, in the US for adults 18 and older.
It rolled out across iOS, Android, the web at muse.ai, and WhatsApp.
Within 13 days, it sat atop the App Store free charts.
Meta has explicitly kept in-app ads out of Muse, at least for now.
Instead, the company is monetizing through subscriptions: a free tier, a $20 per month plan, and a $100 per month premium option.
Muse’s launch didn’t happen on schedule.
Meta originally targeted April 2026 but delayed the rollout to improve safety and reliability.
Intel’s 12% rally deserves its own footnote.
A world where CPU-intensive AI workloads grow faster than expected is arguably the most favorable macro environment Intel could ask for.
Agentic AI, the category Muse belongs to, involves sequential, multi-step tasks: checking your email, cross-referencing your calendar, booking a restaurant, then sending a confirmation.
These workloads are more CPU-intensive than the parallel processing that GPUs excel at.
That distinction matters enormously for companies like AMD and Intel, which have spent years watching Nvidia capture the lion’s share of AI infrastructure spending.

sources.title: Meta’s New Muse Charm Gives Its AI Agent a Gadget of Its Own
passages: Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent.
Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face.
What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live.

Muse already exists across phones, WhatsApp, the web and Macs, and Meta is actively pushing the same agent into its glasses.
That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day.
The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release.
Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet.
Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent.
Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own.
But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important.
Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses.
Still, as strange as an AI Tamagotchi on your keychain might sound, Meta at least isn't starting from scratch.

extraction.body: Meta Muse Charm is a pocket-sized device that gives users direct voice access to the company's existing Muse AI agent without opening a phone or wearing smart glasses. The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release. Unlike earlier standalone AI gadgets, Charm is another access point for an existing Muse agent, with smart-glasses support also on the way. Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent. It's another way to talk to Muse without pulling out your phone or wearing smart glasses, effectively putting the agent on your keychain. Because apparently that's where AI agents live now. The Muse Charm features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen with built-in 5G for on-the-go connectivity, making it more like a tiny standalone computer than an AI-enhanced Tamagotchi. Meta hasn't told us how much something like this will cost, but during Meta Connect 2026, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said we can expect the Muse Charm to ship in time for the holidays in December this year. Muse Charm brings Meta's AI agent into a dedicated pocket-sized device, with more details due before its planned December launch. | Image: Meta Why Would Meta Put Muse on a Keychain? Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet. Which matters, because Meta isn't using the Muse Charm to introduce a brand-new AI assistant. What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live. Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent. It can make purchases, create documents, manage your reminders and interact with services you've connected to Muse, with user approval required for certain actions. One place Muse hasn't reached yet is Meta's smart glasses, though the company says that's coming in the months ahead. Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face. During the unveiling at Meta Connect, Zuckerberg did his best version of Apple's "one more thing", describing the Charm as the quickest way to speak to Muse when you're not wearing Meta's glasses. Right, so it's the second-best option next to Meta's smart glasses. Even as another doorway into the same agent, I'm still scratching my head as to why this was the best form factor for something like this when watches and other wearables are right there. That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day. The agent will receive its own email address, giving you another way to send work its way. In other words, Muse will most certainly "do your emails". But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important. Zuckerberg described the Charm as the quickest way to talk to Muse whenyou'ree not wearing Meta's smart glasses. | Image: Meta Haven't We Tried Dedicated AI Gadgets Before? Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses. So where does the Muse Charm stack up against the AI gadgets that struggled before it? Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own. Muse already exists across phones, WhatsApp, the web and Macs, and Meta is actively pushing the same agent into its glasses. Charm is effectively another access point, not an entirely new ecosystem. Your smartphone already gives you access to plenty of AI agents, while Meta is betting that smart glasses will become the most natural way to talk to one throughout the day. Charm has to prove there is enough friction between those options to justify carrying another device at all. Still, as strange as an AI Tamagotchi on your keychain might sound, Meta at least isn't starting from scratch. Now it just needs to prove it deserves its own gadget.

sources.title: Meta is preparing autonomous Muse Charm device for AI agent — The Verge - UA.NEWS
passages: Meta is developing a standalone device for the new Muse AI agent — the gadget will be called Muse Charm.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg briefly demonstrated it at the end of the Meta Connect presentation.
As The Verge reports , the company plans to ship the device by the December holidays.
Muse Charm resembles a bulky smartwatch without a strap: it has a large screen and a small cord for wearing.
A fingerprint sensor is located in the upper-right corner.
According to Zuckerberg, pressing it will activate the device and allow users to start a conversation with the AI agent.
A small camera is also visible on the body, while there are at least three openings on the front panel, likely for microphones.
Zuckerberg said that using Charm does not require unlocking a phone or opening an app.
At the same time, he did not explain how the device would connect to Meta’s servers.
According to the Meta chief, the company has so far produced only a few such devices and still has to decide on the finishing material.

During the presentation, Zuckerberg also mentioned a semi-transparent outer casing that would make it possible to see the gadget’s internal components, and described the design as styled after hacker aesthetics.

He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.” Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.” Muse is less than a month old, but the AI agent has already become a buzzy new product for Meta.

The bot is capable of taking actions on a user’s behalf, and Zuckerberg dedicated part of tonight’s keynote to new capabilities Meta is adding to the agent, including computer use on Macs and control over an email address.

Meta has a new way to talk to its AI without putting on a pair of glasses.At the end of Wednesday's Meta Connect keynote, CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Muse Charm, a small, always-on handheld device built around Muse, Meta's AI assistant.
Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice.
Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later.The device enters a category with a rocky track record.
Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year.

Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent.
Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face.
What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live.

That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day.
The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release.
Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet.
Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent.
Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own.
But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important.
Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses.

The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release. Unlike earlier standalone AI gadgets, Charm is another access point for an existing Muse agent, with smart-glasses support also on the way. Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent. It's another way to talk to Muse without pulling out your phone or wearing smart glasses, effectively putting the agent on your keychain. Because apparently that's where AI agents live now. The Muse Charm features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen with built-in 5G for on-the-go connectivity, making it more like a tiny standalone computer than an AI-enhanced Tamagotchi. Meta hasn't told us how much something like this will cost, but during Meta Connect 2026, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said we can expect the Muse Charm to ship in time for the holidays in December this year. Muse Charm brings Meta's AI agent into a dedicated pocket-sized device, with more details due before its planned December launch. | Image: Meta Why Would Meta Put Muse on a Keychain? Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet. Which matters, because Meta isn't using the Muse Charm to introduce a brand-new AI assistant. What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live. Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent. It can make purchases, create documents, manage your reminders and interact with services you've connected to Muse, with user approval required for certain actions. One place Muse hasn't reached yet is Meta's smart glasses, though the company says that's coming in the months ahead. Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face. During the unveiling at Meta Connect, Zuckerberg did his best version of Apple's "one more thing", describing the Charm as the quickest way to speak to Muse when you're not wearing Meta's glasses. Right, so it's the second-best option next to Meta's smart glasses. Even as another doorway into the same agent, I'm still scratching my head as to why this was the best form factor for something like this when watches and other wearables are right there. That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day. The agent will receive its own email address, giving you another way to send work its way. In other words, Muse will most certainly "do your emails". But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important. Zuckerberg described the Charm as the quickest way to talk to Muse whenyou'ree not wearing Meta's smart glasses. | Image: Meta Haven't We Tried Dedicated AI Gadgets Before? Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses. So where does the Muse Charm stack up against the AI gadgets that struggled before it? Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own. Muse already exists across phones, WhatsApp, the web and Macs, and Meta is actively pushing the same agent into its glasses. Charm is effectively another access point, not an entirely new ecosystem. Your smartphone already gives you access to plenty of AI agents, while Meta is betting that smart glasses will become the most natural way to talk to one throughout the day. Charm has to prove there is enough friction between those options to justify carrying another device at all. Still, as strange as an AI Tamagotchi on your keychain might sound, Meta at least isn't starting from scratch. Now it just needs to prove it deserves its own gadget.

extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East. passages: Microsoft ( MSFT ) plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the Middle East between now and 2030, the company said September 23, 2026, in a post on its On the Issues blog . The new framework is focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and is organized around three areas: technology, digital resilience, and people. Microsoft said it will pursue the initiatives with partners in the region from now until 2030.

Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations.

Under the technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, building on existing work with HUMAIN , G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait.

The company cited digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. Microsoft said the partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported where relevant and available by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield.

Microsoft said it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region.

The company said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. Describing redundancy as “the foundation of continuity,” Microsoft said that during network disruptions it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers.

On sustainability, Microsoft said that as it expands cloud and AI infrastructure in the four countries it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, guided by the company’s global goals on carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems. Microsoft said it will also work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities for responsible water stewardship across the region and will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment.

Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative built around digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs intended to help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The company said conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty, and that it will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy.

The company will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, complemented by its sovereign-cloud portfolio. Microsoft also said it is deepening partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in the four countries, and that a network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in the four countries will help governments connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft.

Microsoft said it will expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. The company’s AI for Good Lab will continue regional research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.

Under the people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region.

Existing programs cited by the company include Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings.

Microsoft said it will also partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
Microsoft said it has been part of the region’s journey for more than 35 years and is committed to being a partner for the long term.

extraction.body: Feds know of 5 crashes where cars using comma.ai devices hit slow or stopped vehicles. Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously. Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier. (Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.) Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016 . Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves . At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system. Now, Comma says the Comma Four can add lane centering, adaptive cruise, and a cloud-based dash cam to more than 325 models of car across 27 different brands. More than 30,000 drivers are using openpilot, with more than 402 million miles (650 million km) driven. But NHTSA isn’t sure that Comma’s systems are able to adequately detect a slow or stopped car in the path of travel. At least two of the five crashes involved a comma.ai-controlled car hitting a stopped vehicle; in one case, it was a first responder’s vehicle, and the resulting crash killed three. Another of the five crashes saw a comma.ai-controlled car hit a vehicle that was merging, hence this preliminary evaluation. NHTSA says it is also interested in which version of the software was running at the time of each crash—at least two involved forks of the main build, including the fatal crash, which was running a version called FrogPilot . Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a preliminary investigation on September 21 into devices made by Comma AI, the startup founded by security hacker George Hotz, who is no longer managing day-to-day operations but remains a major owner.
Comma AI sells an aftermarket device that brings its driver-assistance system to more than 325 car models.
Comma AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A device that promises hands-off driving for cars people already own is under federal scrutiny.
"ODI has confirmed that the systems were powered on or engaged in multiple crashes," NHTSA wrote.

Regulators said vehicles equipped with the devices struck slow-moving or stopped vehicles in their lanes. "ODI has confirmed that the systems were powered on or engaged in multiple crashes," NHTSA wrote. A state police report said a Toyota RAV4 hit an unoccupied police vehicle that was stopped in a highway lane with its emergency lights on, and two passengers in the Toyota died. In July, NHTSA also issued a broader warning to driverless-vehicle developers about vehicles entering emergency scenes or blocking ambulances and firefighters. Comma AI's own support information lists stationary vehicles in the same lane among conditions that can affect OpenPilot's adaptive cruise control. extraction.body: A device that promises hands-off driving for cars people already own is under federal scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a preliminary investigation on September 21 into devices made by Comma AI, the startup founded by security hacker George Hotz, who is no longer managing day-to-day operations but remains a major owner. Regulators said vehicles equipped with the devices struck slow-moving or stopped vehicles in their lanes. Eleven people were injured, and three people died across the five reported crashes, according to the Office of Defects Investigation. "ODI has confirmed that the systems were powered on or engaged in multiple crashes," NHTSA wrote. "Preliminary data reviewed by ODI suggests that the comma system may not have adequately detected or responded to the in-lane vehicles." Authorities also plan to determine what kind of software was running during each crash, adding that some vehicles may have used modified versions, known as forks, of Comma AI's open-source software. The software in question involves comma three, comma 3X, comma four, and OpenPilot. Comma AI sells an aftermarket device that brings its driver-assistance system to more than 325 car models. The company's website states that the system can steer, accelerate, and brake, and said that it "can drive for hours without intervention." The website also tells drivers to stay alert and ready to take control at any time, and includes a driver-monitoring system that alerts when it detects driver distraction. One crash described in the NHTSA reporting appears to match a February incident in Louisiana. A state police report said a Toyota RAV4 hit an unoccupied police vehicle that was stopped in a highway lane with its emergency lights on, and two passengers in the Toyota died. The police did not identify the driving software in their account of the crash. Other autonomous driving systems and companies have faced investigations over the past few years. NHTSA in 2021 investigated Tesla's Autopilot and said that Teslas using the system struck vehicles stopped at first-responder scenes. There is also an open investigation into Waymo for striking a child near a school in Santa Monica. In July, NHTSA also issued a broader warning to driverless-vehicle developers about vehicles entering emergency scenes or blocking ambulances and firefighters. Comma AI's own support information lists stationary vehicles in the same lane among conditions that can affect OpenPilot's adaptive cruise control. Comma AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

sources.title: YouTube releases new AI features for creators within its Studio app
passages: The draft-feedback feature uses AI to look at a creator’s unpublished video and provide suggestions about pacing, structure, and storytelling.
YouTube is also debuting a new research feed in the Studio app that shows creators what kind of content is working on the platform, so they can apply their own take on it.
YouTube said creators have used its A/B testing feature to run more than 40 million tests on titles and thumbnails.
Soon, the company said, users will be able to test up to three video cuts to see which opening hook works best.
Later this year, YouTube Studio will also automatically monitor thumbnail performance and change one proactively if it doesn’t perform well.

At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their channels, aimed at helping them analyze their videos and grow their audiences.
The updates include expanding Ask Studio, its AI-powered Q&A feature, to iOS and Android, as well as new features that provide feedback on drafts and create dynamic thumbnails.
Creators can also use a new dynamic thumbnail feature to generate three options and show each one to a different segment of their audience.
YouTube also said it’s updating its analytics to go beyond raw numbers, explaining why videos perform the way they do and providing advice about how to make content more engaging.

sources.title: Is YouTube Studio Down? Issues Persist March 30 2026 as Creators Report Analytics and App Glitches
passages: YouTube Studio, the essential dashboard for millions of content creators worldwide, faced scattered access problems and functionality glitches on Monday, March 30, 2026, with users reporting difficulties viewing analytics, subscriber counts and loading certain sections of the mobile app and web interface.As of early afternoon Pacific time, multiple creators took to social media platforms including X to complain that the YouTube Studio app displayed incomplete data, error messages or failed to load tabs properly.

In previous cases, such as the global YouTube disruption on February 17, 2026, the platform attributed problems to backend systems including recommendation algorithms before confirming resolutions within hours.Creators rely heavily on YouTube Studio for daily operations.

Web access to studio.youtube.com showed mixed results, with some creators able to log in normally while others encountered loading delays or missing real-time statistics.This latest round of complaints follows a pattern of YouTube Studio instability earlier in 2026.
Similar glitches were reported in isolated Reddit threads and creator communities in mid-March.YouTube has not issued an official statement specifically addressing Monday's reports as of press time.

For smaller channels and full-time creators, even brief outages can create stress, especially when real-time analytics are unavailable during peak viewing hours.Monday's issues appeared less severe than the March 10 event, which affected loading across both mobile and desktop for many users simultaneously.

Geographic distribution of complaints suggested possible regional variations, though a clear pattern was not immediately evident.YouTube, owned by Google, has expanded its creator tools significantly in recent years to support the platform's more than 2.5 billion monthly users and millions of active channels.

A few shared screenshots showing missing analytics or error screens, urging YouTube to improve communication during technical difficulties.For those unable to access Studio, alternative methods include using third-party analytics tools (where compliant with YouTube's terms) or waiting for mobile app updates.

YouTube periodically rolls out updates to the Studio app that can temporarily introduce or resolve bugs.Looking ahead, industry analysts expect continued enhancements to creator tools, including deeper AI integration for content optimization and monetization insights.
Common issues included subscriber numbers showing as a dash or zero, analytics pages not updating, and generic "something went wrong" prompts when navigating between sections.
On March 10, the platform experienced a widespread partial outage that prevented many creators from accessing their dashboards, triggering panic among some who feared channel termination notices.
YouTube later confirmed the issue was fixed, restoring normal access and accurate statistics.
YouTube's massive scale — processing billions of hours of video daily — makes maintaining 100% uptime a complex engineering challenge.Creators offered mixed reactions online.

While the main YouTube platform for viewers appeared largely unaffected, the creator tools that allow uploading, editing metadata, checking performance and managing channels experienced intermittent disruptions.Downdetector and other outage-tracking sites showed a modest uptick in reports for YouTube-related problems, though not at the scale of major past outages.

However, when core backend services are involved, these steps offer only limited relief.YouTube has invested heavily in creator support infrastructure, including the YouTube Partner Program, dedicated help centers and community forums.
Some expressed frustration at recurring glitches, while others noted that such issues have become somewhat routine and usually resolve quickly.

While not rising to the level of major past outages, the reports highlight ongoing challenges in delivering reliable tools to a global creator base that depends on them for livelihood and audience engagement.As the day progressed, some users noted gradual improvement, with analytics beginning to load or subscriber counts reappearing.

Any disruption draws swift attention because it directly impacts income for those monetizing through ads, memberships, Super Chats and merchandise.Industry observers note that YouTube's rapid feature rollout and heavy reliance on machine learning systems can occasionally lead to backend strain.

Even short disruptions can cascade into lost opportunities, particularly for live streamers or those timing content releases around trending topics.As of Monday afternoon, no widespread confirmation of a full outage had emerged from YouTube.

extraction.body: YouTube has unveiled a host of new features for its content creation platform, YouTube Studio. The updates are aimed at making the creative journey easier and more efficient for creators. The new tools include Ask Studio, an AI-powered feature that provides quick insights on video performance and community feedback. The Ask Studio feature is designed to answer creators' most pressing questions about their content. It can provide insights into analytics, community engagement, and offer new ideas for future videos. The Inspiration tab, on the other hand, helps creators brainstorm by suggesting topics based on audience behavior. The latest update also includes a feature for creators to collaborate on videos. Up to five collaborators can be added to one video, which will be shown to all participating creators' audiences. Additionally, YouTube is improving its auto-dubbing capabilities with new lip sync technology for translated videos across 20 languages. YouTube is also expanding its likeness detection tool to all creators in the YouTube Partner Program. This technology enables creators to detect, manage, and request the removal of unauthorized videos using their facial likeness. The move is part of YouTube's commitment to building AI technology that responsibly empowers human creativity while protecting creators and their businesses from potential misuse or misrepresentation.

passages: YouTube has unveiled a host of new features for its content creation platform, YouTube Studio.
The latest update also includes a feature for creators to collaborate on videos.

extraction.body: YouTube has unveiled a host of new features for its content creation platform, YouTube Studio. The updates are aimed at making the creative journey easier and more efficient for creators. The new tools include Ask Studio, an AI-powered feature that provides quick insights on video performance and community feedback. It also includes an Inspiration tab to spark creativity with suggested topics, title testing for optimizing video titles and thumbnails, and advanced auto dubbing, among other features. The Ask Studio feature is designed to answer creators' most pressing questions about their content. It can provide insights into analytics, community engagement, and offer new ideas for future videos. The Inspiration tab, on the other hand, helps creators brainstorm by suggesting topics based on audience behavior. The latest update also includes a feature for creators to collaborate on videos. Up to five collaborators can be added to one video, which will be shown to all participating creators' audiences. Additionally, YouTube is improving its auto-dubbing capabilities with new lip sync technology for translated videos across 20 languages. YouTube is also expanding its likeness detection tool to all creators in the YouTube Partner Program. This technology enables creators to detect, manage, and request the removal of unauthorized videos using their facial likeness. The move is part of YouTube's commitment to building AI technology that responsibly empowers human creativity while protecting creators and their businesses from potential misuse or misrepresentation.

extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East. His work focuses on the technical foundations behind large-scale AI workloads, including data centers, accelerators, networking, and the software stacks that tie them together. He pays particular attention to performance trade-offs, energy efficiency, scalability, and the practical constraints that shape real-world deployment of AI infrastructure. extraction.body: Microsoft ( MSFT ) plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the Middle East between now and 2030, the company said September 23, 2026, in a post on its On the Issues blog . The new framework is focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and is organized around three areas: technology, digital resilience, and people. Microsoft said it will pursue the initiatives with partners in the region from now until 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Under the technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, building on existing work with HUMAIN , G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. The company cited digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. Microsoft said the partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported where relevant and available by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield. Microsoft said it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. The company said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. Describing redundancy as “the foundation of continuity,” Microsoft said that during network disruptions it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said that as it expands cloud and AI infrastructure in the four countries it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, guided by the company’s global goals on carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems. Microsoft said it will also work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities for responsible water stewardship across the region and will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative built around digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs intended to help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The company said conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty, and that it will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy. The company will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, complemented by its sovereign-cloud portfolio. Microsoft also said it is deepening partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in the four countries, and that a network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in the four countries will help governments connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Microsoft said it will expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. The company’s AI for Good Lab will continue regional research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. Existing programs cited by the company include Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Microsoft said it will also partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. Microsoft said it has been part of the region’s journey for more than 35 years and is committed to being a partner for the long term. Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith and Microsoft Middle East and Africa President Naim Yazbeck today announced a new framework reinforcing Microsoft’s long-term commitment to the Middle East, focused on technology, digital resilience and people.

Unveiled at a round table on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York and attended by senior government representatives from Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the framework includes plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses across the region between now and 2030.

Across the Middle East, governments are pursuing one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations. Realizing this ambition will require digital resilience as a cornerstone, strengthening continuity and recovery, protecting critical data and services, and building trust through stronger cybersecurity.

“Microsoft’s economic ties to the Middle East run deep, and our commitment to the region has always been, and will remain, steadfast. As AI reshapes economies around the world, the Middle East has an important opportunity to lead. Our responsibility is not only to invest in the technology that enables that progress, but to help provide the digital resilience, security and continuity it depends on. This new framework reflects that responsibility and our determination to help the region translate AI ambition into enduring economic and societal benefit,” said Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President, Microsoft.

Naim Yazbeck, President, Microsoft Middle East and Africa, added: “Microsoft has been part of the Middle East’s transformation for more than 35 years, and we’re committed to being here for decades to come. Countries across the region aren’t waiting for the future of AI to be written elsewhere – they’re helping shape it themselves, and our role is to be a long-term partner in that journey. These tangible initiatives expand our commitment as innovation accelerates and national visions advance, strengthening digital resilience, maintaining business continuity and creating lasting opportunity across the region.”

This commitment reflects Microsoft’s belief that every country should be able to benefit from the world’s leading AI and cloud technologies while maintaining confidence in the security, resilience and sovereignty of its digital infrastructure. From now until 2030, Microsoft will pursue the following initiatives with its partners in the region:

As a long-term technology partner to governments, businesses, educators and communities, Microsoft brings together global-scale cloud and AI infrastructure, trusted security and resilience capabilities, and deep local partnerships to help countries advance their national visions. The company will continue working alongside the region to turn AI ambition into lasting economic growth, stronger public services and new opportunities for people.
For additional details, read Brad Smith’s full blog [ here ].

extraction.body: Microsoft on September 23, 2026, announced a new framework for the Middle East focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, saying it plans to invest more than $10 billion in the region through 2030 across technology, digital resilience, and people initiatives. The announcement, published on Microsoft’s On the Issues policy blog, lays out initiatives the company said it will pursue with partners in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since beginning operations there in 1991 and described the region as pursuing “one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations.” Under the framework’s technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the region through 2030. Microsoft said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, naming HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. It pointed to digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. The partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield where relevant and available. The company also plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. Microsoft said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and that it operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft said, it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, and will work with governments and local stakeholders on water stewardship across the region. It also said it will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative offering digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The announcement states that conflict in the region has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. The company said it will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. Those commitments will be complemented by Microsoft’s sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience. Microsoft also announced it is deepening partnerships with cybersecurity authorities in the four countries. A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate those resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across the company. On responsible AI, Microsoft said it will work to strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region, support practical approaches to testing, evaluation, and assurance systems, and expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence , on responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue research and partnerships in the region focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the framework’s people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across the four countries, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions, building on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, the AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the region to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy and helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning. It also said it will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. The announcement closes by noting that Microsoft has been part of the region for more than 35 years and stating that the company is committed to remaining a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educators, and communities across the Middle East.
