extraction.body: Microsoft ( MSFT ) plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses in the Middle East between now and 2030, the company said September 23, 2026, in a post on its On the Issues blog . The new framework is focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and is organized around three areas: technology, digital resilience, and people. Microsoft said it will pursue the initiatives with partners in the region from now until 2030. Microsoft said it has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Under the technology pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. The company said it will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations, building on existing work with HUMAIN , G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait. The company cited digital-government initiatives including TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait. Microsoft said the partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses, supported where relevant and available by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield. Microsoft said it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, an investment it said will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support its growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint in the region. The company said it has invested in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, and operates a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. Describing redundancy as “the foundation of continuity,” Microsoft said that during network disruptions it has rerouted traffic through Middle East corridors and maintained service continuity with minimal impact on customers. On sustainability, Microsoft said that as it expands cloud and AI infrastructure in the four countries it will work with lessor partners to advance its water-positive ambitions, including prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible, guided by the company’s global goals on carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems. Microsoft said it will also work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities for responsible water stewardship across the region and will collaborate with regulators, utilities, and lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. Microsoft said it will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative built around digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs intended to help organizations identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities. The company said conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty, and that it will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy. The company will expand its existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, complemented by its sovereign-cloud portfolio. Microsoft also said it is deepening partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in the four countries, and that a network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in the four countries will help governments connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Microsoft said it will expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation, which it co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools for high-impact AI use cases. The company’s AI for Good Lab will continue regional research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience, including the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities. Under the people pillar, Microsoft said it will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030. The work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. Existing programs cited by the company include Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft said it is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education, including supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Microsoft said it will also partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development, and will engage with workforce coalitions that support national talent strategies and policy recommendations. Microsoft said it has been part of the region’s journey for more than 35 years and is committed to being a partner for the long term. passages: Comparing the revenue trends for BigBear.ai and IONQ provide revealing insights.
Back in 2024, BigBear.ai's quarterly sales towered over IONQ.
This makes sense given the former operates in the hot artificial intelligence sector while the latter focuses on nascent quantum computing technology.
Since then, a dramatic transformation has taken place.
This illustrates the potential for IONQ's business to soar once quantum machines achieve widespread adoption.

Over the observed period, IONQ established a stronger overarching revenue trajectory than BigBear.ai, moving from a lower starting position to surpass its counterpart in the second half of the timeline.

BigBear.ai (NYSE:BBAI) generates most of its revenue by delivering complex artificial intelligence and machine learning decision support tools, focusing heavily on cyber engineering, cloud infrastructure management, and large-scale data processing solutions for a highly specialized client base, particularly the U.S. government.

23, it announced a partnership with AI semiconductor leader Nvidia , where IONQ's latest quantum computer will connect with Nvidia's AI infrastructure to enable "large-scale quantum supercomputers capable of solving the world's hardest problems," according to IONQ.

IONQ (NYSE:IONQ) primarily earns its revenue by constructing general-purpose quantum computing systems and selling commercial access to those computers, facilitating this access both directly and through prominent third-party cloud computing platforms.
Meanwhile, BigBear.ai experienced a year-over-year sales decline in 2025 as the federal government cut budgets.
In Q2 of this year, the company reported 13% revenue growth over 2025 due to its acquisition of Ask Sage, an AI platform tailored to the needs of governments.
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and BigBear.ai wasn’t one of them.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
Before you buy stock in BigBear.ai, consider this:
Robert Izquierdo has positions in IonQ and Nvidia.
Investors evaluating the two companies should watch whether the revenue gap between them continues to widen in upcoming reporting periods or if the comparative trends begin to align more closely.

coreStoryFacts.text: BigBear.ai and Cerebras Systems are capitalizing on the artificial intelligence boom in different ways.
The former is providing AI software primarily to governments, while the latter focuses on specialized semiconductor hardware to deliver superior speed to AI systems.
Examining their revenue trends spell out which is garnering stronger customer adoption.
Cerebras Systems saw the opposite, with revenue rising every quarter until dipping to $180.1 million in Q2.
The recent decline was due to a drop in its hardware sales.
Even so, on a year-over-year basis, Q2 revenue was still higher than in 2025, demonstrating that the company continues to see customer demand for its specialized AI offerings.
The increase was thanks to its acquisition of Ask Sage, an AI platform tailored to the needs of governments.
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and BigBear.ai wasn't one of them.
The 10 stocks that made the cut are built for long-term growth and could produce monster returns in the coming years.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ:CBRS) earns revenue by selling specialized computing hardware and software to data centers and large enterprises.

Revenue serves as a crucial foundational metric that shows investors the total amount of money a business successfully brings in from core day-to-day business operations before any normal operating expenses, corporate taxes, legal costs, or routine overhead charges are deducted.
Comparing the revenue trends for BigBear.ai and IONQ provide revealing insights.
Back in 2024, BigBear.ai's quarterly sales towered over IONQ.
This makes sense given the former operates in the hot artificial intelligence sector while the latter focuses on nascent quantum computing technology.
Since then, a dramatic transformation has taken place.
This illustrates the potential for IONQ's business to soar once quantum machines achieve widespread adoption.

Over the observed period, IONQ established a stronger overarching revenue trajectory than BigBear.ai, moving from a lower starting position to surpass its counterpart in the second half of the timeline.

BigBear.ai (NYSE:BBAI) generates most of its revenue by delivering complex artificial intelligence and machine learning decision support tools, focusing heavily on cyber engineering, cloud infrastructure management, and large-scale data processing solutions for a highly specialized client base, particularly the U.S. government.

23, it announced a partnership with AI semiconductor leader Nvidia , where IONQ's latest quantum computer will connect with Nvidia's AI infrastructure to enable "large-scale quantum supercomputers capable of solving the world's hardest problems," according to IONQ.

IONQ (NYSE:IONQ) primarily earns its revenue by constructing general-purpose quantum computing systems and selling commercial access to those computers, facilitating this access both directly and through prominent third-party cloud computing platforms.
Meanwhile, BigBear.ai experienced a year-over-year sales decline in 2025 as the federal government cut budgets.
In Q2 of this year, the company reported 13% revenue growth over 2025 due to its acquisition of Ask Sage, an AI platform tailored to the needs of governments.

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. sources.title: Meta’s New Muse Charm Gives Its AI Agent a Gadget of Its Own
passages: Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent.
Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face.
What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live.
Zuckerberg described the Charm as the quickest way to talk to Muse whenyou'ree not wearing Meta's smart glasses. | Image: Meta Haven't We Tried Dedicated AI Gadgets Before?
Muse already exists across phones, WhatsApp, the web and Macs, and Meta is actively pushing the same agent into its glasses.
That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day.
The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release.
Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet.
Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent.
Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own.
But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important.
Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses.
Still, as strange as an AI Tamagotchi on your keychain might sound, Meta at least isn't starting from scratch.

extraction.body: Meta Muse Charm is a pocket-sized device that gives users direct voice access to the company's existing Muse AI agent without opening a phone or wearing smart glasses. The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release. Unlike earlier standalone AI gadgets, Charm is another access point for an existing Muse agent, with smart-glasses support also on the way. Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent. It's another way to talk to Muse without pulling out your phone or wearing smart glasses, effectively putting the agent on your keychain. Because apparently that's where AI agents live now. The Muse Charm features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen with built-in 5G for on-the-go connectivity, making it more like a tiny standalone computer than an AI-enhanced Tamagotchi. Meta hasn't told us how much something like this will cost, but during Meta Connect 2026, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said we can expect the Muse Charm to ship in time for the holidays in December this year. Muse Charm brings Meta's AI agent into a dedicated pocket-sized device, with more details due before its planned December launch. | Image: Meta Why Would Meta Put Muse on a Keychain? Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet. Which matters, because Meta isn't using the Muse Charm to introduce a brand-new AI assistant. What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live. Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent. It can make purchases, create documents, manage your reminders and interact with services you've connected to Muse, with user approval required for certain actions. One place Muse hasn't reached yet is Meta's smart glasses, though the company says that's coming in the months ahead. Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face. During the unveiling at Meta Connect, Zuckerberg did his best version of Apple's "one more thing", describing the Charm as the quickest way to speak to Muse when you're not wearing Meta's glasses. Right, so it's the second-best option next to Meta's smart glasses. Even as another doorway into the same agent, I'm still scratching my head as to why this was the best form factor for something like this when watches and other wearables are right there. That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day. The agent will receive its own email address, giving you another way to send work its way. In other words, Muse will most certainly "do your emails". But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important. Zuckerberg described the Charm as the quickest way to talk to Muse whenyou'ree not wearing Meta's smart glasses. | Image: Meta Haven't We Tried Dedicated AI Gadgets Before? Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses. So where does the Muse Charm stack up against the AI gadgets that struggled before it? Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own. Muse already exists across phones, WhatsApp, the web and Macs, and Meta is actively pushing the same agent into its glasses. Charm is effectively another access point, not an entirely new ecosystem. Your smartphone already gives you access to plenty of AI agents, while Meta is betting that smart glasses will become the most natural way to talk to one throughout the day. Charm has to prove there is enough friction between those options to justify carrying another device at all. Still, as strange as an AI Tamagotchi on your keychain might sound, Meta at least isn't starting from scratch. Now it just needs to prove it deserves its own gadget.

sources.title: Meta’s New Muse Charm Gives Its AI Agent a Gadget of Its Own
passages: Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent.
Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face.
What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live.
Zuckerberg described the Charm as the quickest way to talk to Muse whenyou'ree not wearing Meta's smart glasses. | Image: Meta Haven't We Tried Dedicated AI Gadgets Before?
Muse already exists across phones, WhatsApp, the web and Macs, and Meta is actively pushing the same agent into its glasses.
That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day.
The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release.
Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet.
Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent.
Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own.
But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important.
Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses.
Still, as strange as an AI Tamagotchi on your keychain might sound, Meta at least isn't starting from scratch.

extraction.body: Meta Muse Charm is a pocket-sized device that gives users direct voice access to the company's existing Muse AI agent without opening a phone or wearing smart glasses. The device features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen and built-in 5G, with Meta targeting a December 2026 release. Unlike earlier standalone AI gadgets, Charm is another access point for an existing Muse agent, with smart-glasses support also on the way. Meta took one look at Bandai's Tamagotchi Smart Ring and said, "Hold my virtual beer." Let Meta present the new Muse Charm, a pocket-sized device built around the company's recently launched Muse AI agent. It's another way to talk to Muse without pulling out your phone or wearing smart glasses, effectively putting the agent on your keychain. Because apparently that's where AI agents live now. The Muse Charm features a roughly 2-inch touchscreen with built-in 5G for on-the-go connectivity, making it more like a tiny standalone computer than an AI-enhanced Tamagotchi. Meta hasn't told us how much something like this will cost, but during Meta Connect 2026, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said we can expect the Muse Charm to ship in time for the holidays in December this year. Muse Charm brings Meta's AI agent into a dedicated pocket-sized device, with more details due before its planned December launch. | Image: Meta Why Would Meta Put Muse on a Keychain? Unless you've been keeping close tabs on Meta's latest AI push, there's a decent chance Muse hasn't crossed your radar yet. Which matters, because Meta isn't using the Muse Charm to introduce a brand-new AI assistant. What this device actually does is give Meta's existing Muse personal AI agent another place to live. Muse does a lot of the things you'd expect from an AI agent. It can make purchases, create documents, manage your reminders and interact with services you've connected to Muse, with user approval required for certain actions. One place Muse hasn't reached yet is Meta's smart glasses, though the company says that's coming in the months ahead. Basically, the whole idea behind the Muse Charm is to make that same agent easier to reach when you don't want to open an app or wear Meta hardware on your face. During the unveiling at Meta Connect, Zuckerberg did his best version of Apple's "one more thing", describing the Charm as the quickest way to speak to Muse when you're not wearing Meta's glasses. Right, so it's the second-best option next to Meta's smart glasses. Even as another doorway into the same agent, I'm still scratching my head as to why this was the best form factor for something like this when watches and other wearables are right there. That said, Meta is expanding what Muse can do day-to-day. The agent will receive its own email address, giving you another way to send work its way. In other words, Muse will most certainly "do your emails". But with a Charm clipped to your keychain, you'll be talking to it before sending the agent off to do those things elsewhere while you get on with something more important. Zuckerberg described the Charm as the quickest way to talk to Muse whenyou'ree not wearing Meta's smart glasses. | Image: Meta Haven't We Tried Dedicated AI Gadgets Before? Meta is stepping into an unstable playing field, with standalone AI hardware not exactly impressing the masses. So where does the Muse Charm stack up against the AI gadgets that struggled before it? Well, Meta isn't asking the device to establish an entirely new AI platform on its own. Muse already exists across phones, WhatsApp, the web and Macs, and Meta is actively pushing the same agent into its glasses. Charm is effectively another access point, not an entirely new ecosystem. Your smartphone already gives you access to plenty of AI agents, while Meta is betting that smart glasses will become the most natural way to talk to one throughout the day. Charm has to prove there is enough friction between those options to justify carrying another device at all. Still, as strange as an AI Tamagotchi on your keychain might sound, Meta at least isn't starting from scratch. Now it just needs to prove it deserves its own gadget.

sources.title: What To Expect At Meta Connect 2026: New AI Glasses, A Mixed Reality Headset And More - Engadget
passages: It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect.
Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon.
Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display .
There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI.

And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year.
Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors.
I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse .
More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses.
Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others.
In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect.

Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility.
The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote.
I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem.
Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 .
These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant.

Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover.

extraction.body: There's a lot for Mark Zuckerberg to cover at this year's keynote. Meta is about to hold its biggest event of the year. While Connect was once solely dedicated to virtual reality, the event now covers all the company's hardware projects, as well as AI and the metaverse. And this year could be even more jam-packed than usual. Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover. Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 . There will be additional talks and developer sessions the following day, starting with a 10AM PT/1PM ET "developer state of the union." As usual, I'll be on the ground watching the keynote live from Meta's HQ in Menlo Park so check back for our liveblog and post-keynote coverage. In the meantime, here's everything I'll be looking out for during Connect. As with the last few years, there's likely to be a lot of glasses-related news. One interesting change with this year's strategy is that the company is reportedly working on a pair of camera-free frames . These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant. The lack of cameras could offer Meta a couple of advantages. The frames will reportedly be a bit slimmer and look more like "normal glasses." More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses. Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others. In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect. Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon. That could be a reference to these camera-free frames or, perhaps, a new Gen 3 lineup (the first Gen 2 models debuted at last year's Connect). Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display . There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI. But it's been a while since we've heard anything about the rumored device, sometimes called "Hypernova 2," so Meta could be holding that one back for now. It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect. Several images of the lightweight device recently surfaced in a HorizonOS update. Those images show a thin device that almost looks more like a pair of goggles than a headset. It also clearly shows a cable, which supports previous reporting that Phoenix will rely on a tethered connection to a separate puck. It's also rumored to support hand and eye tracking rather than a dedicated controller. And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year. Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors. A new kind of headset will probably also mean some updates to HorizonOS, and it will be interesting to see what kinds of experiences Meta will promote alongside the new hardware. The company has been shuttering VR studios left and right, so I doubt we would see any huge game announcements to go with Phoenix. But it does seem like Meta could promote more entertainment-focused offerings. Deadline reported last year that Meta was backing a new "3D horror series" based on A24's Talk to Me that's apparently meant for viewing in the company's headsets. We may also hear more about Meta's holographic avatars that we first saw two years ago with its Orion prototype. Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility. The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote. These avatars could also factor into Meta's evolving vision for the metaverse. When the company almost shut down Horizon Worlds in VR earlier this year, Bosworth said that augmented reality was very much part of the company's "expansive construct of the metaverse." The last few years of Connect have included a lot of AI news and this year shouldn't be any different. This will be the first Connect since we've seen a flood of new AI releases from the company's superintelligence group, and I'm sure the company is saving some AI-focused updates for Connect. I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse . The company teased that glasses support for the agent would be coming "soon," so I wouldn't be surprised if we hear more about how this will work at Connect. (Agent capabilities could also be a good selling point for camera-free glasses.) I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem. Last year at Connect, the company announced a handful of apps that would be coming to its camera glasses, but we haven't seen a whole lot of momentum since. And earlier this year it started allowing developers to create dedicated apps for Meta Ray-Ban Display. Showing off a new slate of third-party apps for the frames could be a good way to build more excitement for the product even if we don't see updated hardware.

passages: It’s time once again for Meta’s annual September product launch event, and The Verge is on the ground in Menlo Park to cover the show live.
Meta says that today’s keynote by Mark Zuckerberg will be about how “Meta is building a future for everyone” — something he wrote at length about in a recent essay about AI, smart glasses, and more.

The company is dealing with an outpouring of privacy and harassment concerns stemming from the product line’s built-in camera, which has led to them being derided as “pervert glasses.” Meta has already tried to tackle that reputation with recent privacy fixes and a new marketing campaign, but it could introduce more updates on the Connect stage.
That means we can expect more news from Zuckerberg and his team on those topics; perhaps we’ll hear more about Meta’s recently launched Muse AI agent and new glasses hardware.

extraction.body: There's a lot for Mark Zuckerberg to cover at this year's keynote. Meta is about to hold its biggest event of the year. While Connect was once solely dedicated to virtual reality, the event now covers all the company's hardware projects, as well as AI and the metaverse. And this year could be even more jam-packed than usual. Between Meta's ever-expanding smart glasses lineup, its breakneck AI releases and the current industry freakout over the pace of AI development, there's certainly a lot of ground for CEO Mark Zuckerberg to cover. Like last year's event, Meta has again opted for an evening keynote, with Zuckerberg taking the stage at 4PM PT/7PM ET on September 23 . There will be additional talks and developer sessions the following day, starting with a 10AM PT/1PM ET "developer state of the union." As usual, I'll be on the ground watching the keynote live from Meta's HQ in Menlo Park so check back for our liveblog and post-keynote coverage. In the meantime, here's everything I'll be looking out for during Connect. As with the last few years, there's likely to be a lot of glasses-related news. One interesting change with this year's strategy is that the company is reportedly working on a pair of camera-free frames . These glasses, which will reportedly come in two styles, will instead come with extra microphones for chatting with Meta's AI assistant. The lack of cameras could offer Meta a couple of advantages. The frames will reportedly be a bit slimmer and look more like "normal glasses." More significantly, they could also help Meta address ongoing privacy concerns and backlash against its current lineup of glasses. Meta has been trying to get ahead of the "creep glasses" narrative in recent weeks by cracking down on people who tamper with the LED lights and post videos of themselves harassing others. In a recent AMA on Instagram , Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said the company would have "more to say" about the issue during Connect. Ray-Ban has recently hinted that it has new Meta-branded glasses coming soon. That could be a reference to these camera-free frames or, perhaps, a new Gen 3 lineup (the first Gen 2 models debuted at last year's Connect). Another possibility is the next generation of Meta Ray-Ban Display . There have been reports that Meta is working on a version of the glasses that will come with displays in both lenses, which would open up some interesting possibilities in terms of their UI. But it's been a while since we've heard anything about the rumored device, sometimes called "Hypernova 2," so Meta could be holding that one back for now. It's been a while since we've seen a new headset from Meta, and we've never seen anything from them quite like the device currently known as "Phoenix." The mixed reality headset has been rumored for some time, but it certainly seems like the company is gearing up for it to make its official debut at Connect. Several images of the lightweight device recently surfaced in a HorizonOS update. Those images show a thin device that almost looks more like a pair of goggles than a headset. It also clearly shows a cable, which supports previous reporting that Phoenix will rely on a tethered connection to a separate puck. It's also rumored to support hand and eye tracking rather than a dedicated controller. And while we don't know much about what Phoenix will look like in the way of specs, it seems like a pretty good bet the headset will be among the first devices to use the new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip Qualcomm announced earlier this year. Intended for mixed reality headsets, the chip was specifically designed to support slimmed-down form factors. A new kind of headset will probably also mean some updates to HorizonOS, and it will be interesting to see what kinds of experiences Meta will promote alongside the new hardware. The company has been shuttering VR studios left and right, so I doubt we would see any huge game announcements to go with Phoenix. But it does seem like Meta could promote more entertainment-focused offerings. Deadline reported last year that Meta was backing a new "3D horror series" based on A24's Talk to Me that's apparently meant for viewing in the company's headsets. We may also hear more about Meta's holographic avatars that we first saw two years ago with its Orion prototype. Meta told me at the time that the technology would eventually come to virtual reality and, given that Qualcomm has highlighted "photorealistic avatars" as one of the benefits of its aforementioned chip, this seems like a very real possibility. The Information also recently reported that an avatar of Meta's CTO could make an appearance during the Connect keynote. These avatars could also factor into Meta's evolving vision for the metaverse. When the company almost shut down Horizon Worlds in VR earlier this year, Bosworth said that augmented reality was very much part of the company's "expansive construct of the metaverse." The last few years of Connect have included a lot of AI news and this year shouldn't be any different. This will be the first Connect since we've seen a flood of new AI releases from the company's superintelligence group, and I'm sure the company is saving some AI-focused updates for Connect. I fully expect Meta to talk a lot more about its AI agent, Muse . The company teased that glasses support for the agent would be coming "soon," so I wouldn't be surprised if we hear more about how this will work at Connect. (Agent capabilities could also be a good selling point for camera-free glasses.) I'm also hoping to hear more about Meta's work to bring more third-party apps to its glasses ecosystem. Last year at Connect, the company announced a handful of apps that would be coming to its camera glasses, but we haven't seen a whole lot of momentum since. And earlier this year it started allowing developers to create dedicated apps for Meta Ray-Ban Display. Showing off a new slate of third-party apps for the frames could be a good way to build more excitement for the product even if we don't see updated hardware.

Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99.
These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.

Moments before unveiling them, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile ago to shift its focus away from the Metaverse and build fewer VR devices until it had real breakthroughs.

"This is a breakthrough," he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. "A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we've also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time."

Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before. The frames are made of magnesium alloy, and the glasses are powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They connect to a computing puck that doubles as a battery, which users can just slip the puck into their pocket to use the glasses on the go.

The glasses are largely built for entertainment. Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support. Users will be able to download and watch movies.
Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.

Indeed, the company calls the glasses the "first IMAX-enhanced certified VR device ever" and says they will be one of the few ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines IMAX's distinct high-resolution viewing experience.

The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user's physical space into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D.

Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings "transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio" — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience.

The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you'll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.

passages: In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset.
Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas.
Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9.

A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles.
The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it.

Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie.

Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.
The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets.
Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock.

However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around.

Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.
That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer.
There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled.
Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby.

A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles. The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it. However, the reveal of Meta’s new entertainment-centric gizmo, Meta VR Glasses, arriving this spring, might just be enough of a departure to entice agonistics like myself, starting with the fact that wearing them doesn’t make you feel like you’re in an episode of Black Mirror. They are, for all intents and purposes, a pair of slick dark glasses. They still have the noticeable bulge of a VR device, but they’re more along the lines of X-Men’s Cyclops than Johnny Mnemonic . These streamlined shades feature a cable leading to a “puck” the size of an iPhone, a battery-and-computer pack you can place in your pocket or handbag, or clip to your belt. Its 45W fast-charging will probably come in handy, since it only holds enough juice for three hours of continuous playback, but the dangling accessory isn’t too obtrusive a trade-off, given the device’s larger, heavier predecessors. The glasses themselves weigh only about a hundred grams — a quarter of a pound — compared to the five to six hundred grams of the Meta Quest. The biggest upgrade from the Meta Quest, however, is the complete lack of hand-held controllers and the reliance on physical gestures instead. Apple’s equivalent already has this, but the Meta VR Glasses offer the chance to use these flicks and pinches without feeling like you’re in a Saw trap. The initial adjustments seem pretty easy, between switchable nose pads of different sizes and lenses you can slide left and right to ensure they’re at the correct distance. There’s no official info on what to do if you wear glasses just yet, but some leaks out there suggest prescription lens capability is the plan. Tiny cameras alongside the glasses' stems capture minor movements, like using your thumb to imitate scrolling on a touch remote, or pinching an invisible button, which in turn trigger and toggle menus affixed to the space around you. The cameras on the front re-create your regular vision, with a bit of a catch. The world around you gets noticeably noisier (as in, filled with digital noise) and the frame rate doesn’t exactly sync up with fluorescent lightbulbs, so you might see a bit of a flicker when looking past the floating UX at actual surfaces. Navigating the real world will still probably be a challenge, and the tech’s hologram features (and spatial audio) for video calling weren’t part of the demo. However, Meta VR Glasses feel aimed at sitting down to watch movies and TV rather than augmenting reality. With its 5K display made of micro OLED panels, 37 pixels per degree, and Dolby Vision enhancements, you’re getting a pretty high-quality image, and navigating it is gamified too. Once you sync your eye movements to the cursor, simply looking at an app icon will light it up. Just pinch to select. But what about the actual offerings? Well, that’s where things get interesting. In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset. Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9. With films like The Odyssey , Sinners and Dune: Part Three reflecting an increased demand for the format, which can’t fully be met, this is the next best thing. But what does actually watching a movie in one of these look like? Well, you have a couple of options. For most films, a screen pops up at a certain distance, which you’ll eventually be able to move back or forth. This feature wasn’t yet available, leaving part of the screen outside the glasses’ field of view, which isn’t ideal, but it’s still early days since the product is several months away from release. Your second option, for select films and experiences, is an “Immersive Cinema” virtual reality viewing room by ILM, built in sync with the movie itself. For this Disney+ demo, I picked Avengers: Infinity War — specifically, the scene where Thor harnesses the power of a dying star to forge his new hammer, Stormbreaker. If you’ve ever fantasized about watching a movie while seated in a grungy space factory as lava splashes from around the screen, you’re in luck. For Marvel and Star Wars offerings, environments like Tatooine and Avengers Tower appear to be in the works. The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets. Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock. However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around. This isn’t magic; the folks at Meta had cameras appropriately placed to capture the effect, so future games will have to be equipped for this sort of broadcast if you want to, say, wave at Spike Lee as he jumps around euphorically. Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through. The speakers on the glasses — which you can control using tiny buttons along the bottoms of the stems — provide a fairly immersive surround sound experience courtesy of Dolby Atmos. This comes in handy for playing music-based games like Beat Saber, one of 75 built-in games available at launch (this particular version was enhanced for the device’s handsfree capabilities) in addition to the XBOX Cloud Gaming, i.e. streaming games directly to your headset. You also have the option of scrolling social media, and typing on a nifty keyboard projected on flat surfaces in front of you, as you look down at your digital ghost hands and their spectral glow. The novelty will probably wear off after a while, but at first, it’s pretty thrilling if you’ve never used this kind of technology before — which appears to be the target market for Meta VR Glasses. Of course, there’s a work capability too; you can mirror your Mac or PC into this virtual space, either wirelessly or via USB-C. On the other hand, the device’s $1,299.99 price tag — more than a solid TV and Blu-ray player combined — might be a deterrent to the average consumer who hasn’t yet dipped their toe into VR. That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer. The only way to be remotely convinced of the technology is to experience it for yourself, which a re-creation on a flat screen (say, a YouTube video) can’t fully convey. There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled. There are kinks that still need to be worked out by launch, like the glare from light sources behind you leaking into your field of view (perhaps the one downside to opening up those goggles), but a head tilt here or there can probably solve that issue. Also not part of the tech demo was the ability to re-orient where exactly in your horizontal field of view a given screen appears, but this was something Meta’s engineers demonstrated for us on the fly, with the promise that we’d eventually be able to do it ourselves. Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby. Look, it can be hard to trust big tech in our increasingly dystopian world, and who knows what data this particular chapter of the company will try to harness or sell. But the lineup of streaming services and viewing features on offer makes Meta VR Glasses one of the more intriguing developments in the field if you’re unsure about stepping into virtual spaces. Compared to existing devices on the market, the openness of the design — which still allows you to peek out from time to time and go back to the real world pretty easily — makes for the kind of compromise that fence-sitters like myself might just be able to accept. If nothing else, it’s more convenient, and slightly less embarrassing, than buying a scalped IMAX ticket on eBay.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing.
At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99.
Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.
Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before.
Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support.
Users will be able to download and watch movies.
The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience.
Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.
These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.

So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.”

Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas.

The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it.

Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie.

Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.
The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets.
Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock.

However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around.

Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.
That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer.
There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled.
Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby.

These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility. Moments before unveiling them, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile ago to shift its focus away from the Metaverse and build fewer VR devices until it had real breakthroughs. “This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. The frames are made of magnesium alloy, and the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They connect to a computing puck that doubles as a battery, which users can just slip the puck into their pocket to use the glasses on the go. The glasses are largely built for entertainment. Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support. Users will be able to download and watch movies. Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films. Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX-enhanced certified VR device ever” and says they will be one of the few ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines IMAX’s distinct high-resolution viewing experience. The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D. Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience. The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9.

A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles.
The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it.

Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie.

Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor.
The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets.
Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock.

However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around.

Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through.
That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer.
There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled.
Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby.

extraction.body: Tech companies have gradually invaded the film festival space, but Meta’s secret new project was a perfect fit for this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, both because of its entertainment capabilities, and because it feels straight out of a movie. Not far from where I’d soon watch the new Zack Snyder film , a makeshift gallery played host to covert keynote presentations, each with an audience of one, as a well-dressed entertainment executive showed surprising candor. “We are… self-aware,” she sighed. A strange way to begin a marketing pitch, but a surprisingly welcome one, as she echoed thoughts that have likely been on the mind of anyone who has thus far rejected the industry’s clunky VR-sphere, and its closed-off headsets akin to ski goggles. The Meta Quest (and like it, the Apple Vision Pro) haven’t exactly pivoted society towards Ready Player One, and perhaps we’re better for it. However, the reveal of Meta’s new entertainment-centric gizmo, Meta VR Glasses, arriving this spring, might just be enough of a departure to entice agonistics like myself, starting with the fact that wearing them doesn’t make you feel like you’re in an episode of Black Mirror. They are, for all intents and purposes, a pair of slick dark glasses. They still have the noticeable bulge of a VR device, but they’re more along the lines of X-Men’s Cyclops than Johnny Mnemonic . These streamlined shades feature a cable leading to a “puck” the size of an iPhone, a battery-and-computer pack you can place in your pocket or handbag, or clip to your belt. Its 45W fast-charging will probably come in handy, since it only holds enough juice for three hours of continuous playback, but the dangling accessory isn’t too obtrusive a trade-off, given the device’s larger, heavier predecessors. The glasses themselves weigh only about a hundred grams — a quarter of a pound — compared to the five to six hundred grams of the Meta Quest. The biggest upgrade from the Meta Quest, however, is the complete lack of hand-held controllers and the reliance on physical gestures instead. Apple’s equivalent already has this, but the Meta VR Glasses offer the chance to use these flicks and pinches without feeling like you’re in a Saw trap. The initial adjustments seem pretty easy, between switchable nose pads of different sizes and lenses you can slide left and right to ensure they’re at the correct distance. There’s no official info on what to do if you wear glasses just yet, but some leaks out there suggest prescription lens capability is the plan. Tiny cameras alongside the glasses' stems capture minor movements, like using your thumb to imitate scrolling on a touch remote, or pinching an invisible button, which in turn trigger and toggle menus affixed to the space around you. The cameras on the front re-create your regular vision, with a bit of a catch. The world around you gets noticeably noisier (as in, filled with digital noise) and the frame rate doesn’t exactly sync up with fluorescent lightbulbs, so you might see a bit of a flicker when looking past the floating UX at actual surfaces. Navigating the real world will still probably be a challenge, and the tech’s hologram features (and spatial audio) for video calling weren’t part of the demo. However, Meta VR Glasses feel aimed at sitting down to watch movies and TV rather than augmenting reality. With its 5K display made of micro OLED panels, 37 pixels per degree, and Dolby Vision enhancements, you’re getting a pretty high-quality image, and navigating it is gamified too. Once you sync your eye movements to the cursor, simply looking at an app icon will light it up. Just pinch to select. But what about the actual offerings? Well, that’s where things get interesting. In addition to all your streaming favorites (Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, and vitally, Tubi), Meta has teamed up with IMAX to bring the world of full-frame, 1:43:1 IMAX movies to your headset. Currently, this is poised to be the only way to watch something like The Odyssey in its native aspect ratio outside of a handful of cinemas. Sadly, that option wasn’t available during our limited tech demo, but it sets Meta VR Glasses apart even from Blu-ray and UHD, which only expand to the size of your HD television — a paltry 16:9. With films like The Odyssey , Sinners and Dune: Part Three reflecting an increased demand for the format, which can’t fully be met, this is the next best thing. But what does actually watching a movie in one of these look like? Well, you have a couple of options. For most films, a screen pops up at a certain distance, which you’ll eventually be able to move back or forth. This feature wasn’t yet available, leaving part of the screen outside the glasses’ field of view, which isn’t ideal, but it’s still early days since the product is several months away from release. Your second option, for select films and experiences, is an “Immersive Cinema” virtual reality viewing room by ILM, built in sync with the movie itself. For this Disney+ demo, I picked Avengers: Infinity War — specifically, the scene where Thor harnesses the power of a dying star to forge his new hammer, Stormbreaker. If you’ve ever fantasized about watching a movie while seated in a grungy space factory as lava splashes from around the screen, you’re in luck. For Marvel and Star Wars offerings, environments like Tatooine and Avengers Tower appear to be in the works. The 3D isn’t too bad either (as evidenced by a short clip of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness), though the effect is no more or less immersive than most current 3D television sets. Upon launch, 3D offerings will be available from the likes of HBO Max, Paramount+ and Peacock. However, where things get really novel is the switch from movies to sports, where you have the option of not just watching your game of choice with a 180-degree field of view — in this case, Game 4 of the 2026 NBA finals; go Knicks — but sitting in a variety of courtside seats and glancing around. This isn’t magic; the folks at Meta had cameras appropriately placed to capture the effect, so future games will have to be equipped for this sort of broadcast if you want to, say, wave at Spike Lee as he jumps around euphorically. Then again, between the NBA finals and the FIFA World Cup, if this summer has proved anything, it’s that sports are a social event, so closing yourself off this way might at best be a backup for plans that fall through. The speakers on the glasses — which you can control using tiny buttons along the bottoms of the stems — provide a fairly immersive surround sound experience courtesy of Dolby Atmos. This comes in handy for playing music-based games like Beat Saber, one of 75 built-in games available at launch (this particular version was enhanced for the device’s handsfree capabilities) in addition to the XBOX Cloud Gaming, i.e. streaming games directly to your headset. You also have the option of scrolling social media, and typing on a nifty keyboard projected on flat surfaces in front of you, as you look down at your digital ghost hands and their spectral glow. The novelty will probably wear off after a while, but at first, it’s pretty thrilling if you’ve never used this kind of technology before — which appears to be the target market for Meta VR Glasses. Of course, there’s a work capability too; you can mirror your Mac or PC into this virtual space, either wirelessly or via USB-C. On the other hand, the device’s $1,299.99 price tag — more than a solid TV and Blu-ray player combined — might be a deterrent to the average consumer who hasn’t yet dipped their toe into VR. That is, unless Meta plans to roll out highly involved tech demos for every potential buyer. The only way to be remotely convinced of the technology is to experience it for yourself, which a re-creation on a flat screen (say, a YouTube video) can’t fully convey. There’s a candy store feeling to wearing one of these and turning around to see a fully (or semi) rendered space behind you, waiting to be filled. There are kinks that still need to be worked out by launch, like the glare from light sources behind you leaking into your field of view (perhaps the one downside to opening up those goggles), but a head tilt here or there can probably solve that issue. Also not part of the tech demo was the ability to re-orient where exactly in your horizontal field of view a given screen appears, but this was something Meta’s engineers demonstrated for us on the fly, with the promise that we’d eventually be able to do it ourselves. Much like legs in the Metaverse, it’s coming, baby. Look, it can be hard to trust big tech in our increasingly dystopian world, and who knows what data this particular chapter of the company will try to harness or sell. But the lineup of streaming services and viewing features on offer makes Meta VR Glasses one of the more intriguing developments in the field if you’re unsure about stepping into virtual spaces. Compared to existing devices on the market, the openness of the design — which still allows you to peek out from time to time and go back to the real world pretty easily — makes for the kind of compromise that fence-sitters like myself might just be able to accept. If nothing else, it’s more convenient, and slightly less embarrassing, than buying a scalped IMAX ticket on eBay.

sources.title: Gov. JB Pritzker assembling Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess AI threats - Chicago Sun-Times
passages: The Democratic governor signed an executive order Tuesday establishing the Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess “the various risks posed by Al to the safety of Illinois residents and the critical infrastructure residents rely on.”

JB Pritzker is convening a panel of experts to advise state officials on the potential threats of artificial intelligence as a growing number of industry leaders warn the burgeoning, self-improving technology could spell doomsday for humanity if left unchecked.

Pritzker will name his AI Cabinet members “in the coming weeks” to work alongside numerous state agency leaders, including from the Department of Innovation and Technology, the Department of Public Health and the Illinois Emergency Management Agency.
“Illinois has already enacted nation-leading laws that hold Big Tech accountable and today I’m taking executive action to keep this a priority,” Pritzker said.

They’re expected to come from backgrounds in academia, law, ethics and governance, and provide recommendations on potential public safety threats, protecting public assets and evaluating possible regulations, according to Pritzker’s office.
From WBUR and NPR, co-hosted by Robin Young and Scott Tong, with news from Chicago from WBEZ’s Lisa Labuz.

JB Pritzker is convening a panel of experts to advise state officials on the potential threats of artificial intelligence as a growing number of industry leaders warn the burgeoning, self-improving technology could spell doomsday for humanity if left unchecked. The Democratic governor signed an executive order Tuesday establishing the Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess “the various risks posed by Al to the safety of Illinois residents and the critical infrastructure residents rely on.” Pritzker will name his AI Cabinet members “in the coming weeks” to work alongside numerous state agency leaders, including from the Department of Innovation and Technology, the Department of Public Health and the Illinois Emergency Management Agency. They’re expected to come from backgrounds in academia, law, ethics and governance, and provide recommendations on potential public safety threats, protecting public assets and evaluating possible regulations, according to Pritzker’s office. extraction.body: SPRINGFIELD — Gov. JB Pritzker is setting up a new group within state government to explore more regulations for artificial intelligence as calls grow across the country for new restrictions. Pritzker signed an executive order on Tuesday to establish an AI Cabinet made up of experts and representatives from several state agencies. The unpaid group, which will formulate policy proposals through 2027, will analyze and assess “the various risks posed by AI to the safety of Illinois residents and the critical infrastructure residents rely on.” It’s the latest move by Illinois to tackle state-focused AI regulation as the federal government continues to take a hands-off approach , even as industry insiders sound the alarm on the technology’s capabilities. A former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher alleged in an explosive social media post earlier this month that AI companies are building a tool that could become “out of control” and pose a threat to human existence by 2030. “Artificial Intelligence has enormous potential to transform our everyday lives, but when experts and industry leaders sound the alarm bell, urge us to slow down, and ask for guardrails, we should listen,” Pritzker said in a statement. The cabinet will formulate policies and procedures to protect Illinois residents and public assets like water systems, education and information systems from threats posed by AI. It will also analyze “emerging AI incidents and share lessons learned” from them. The advisory group will also make policy recommendations on risk management and assess the feasibility, timeframe and any other challenges for implementing them. The cabinet will consider regulations tying data center incentives or operational approval to a company’s ability to meet safety, accountability and transparency standards. It will also look into addressing strain on the energy grid from data centers, evaluating how state procurement and contracting practices can incorporate AI safety and accountability measures, and assessing if existing legal options are good enough to hold AI companies that cause harm accountable. Illinois lawmakers have already taken steps to regulate AI. Pritzker signed Senate Bill 315 in July, also known as the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act , which increases transparency and accountability requirements for the largest artificial intelligence models — those that generate more than $500 million in annual revenue and are trained using massive computing power. It establishes new reporting standards for the possibility that the AI model could be used for large-scale harm, such as by helping create a chemical, biological or nuclear weapon or committing cyber-attacks. It also made Illinois the first state to require annual audits of AI. The law takes effect in 2028. Since the whistleblower came forward earlier this month, Pritzker has been aggressively calling on Congress to step in. “It should be among the top priorities, but don't misunderstand, it is dangerous and it's dangerous on the level of nuclear weapons,” Pritzker said on ABC’s Sunday morning news show . “So that's why it needs to be an international endeavor. Pritzker has urged Congress to immediately begin holding hearings on AI safety and impose national standards.
