Gov. JB Pritzker speaks at the signing of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Safety Measures Act in the Loop July 6.

Gov. JB Pritzker is convening a panel of experts to advise state officials on the potential threats of artificial intelligence as a growing number of industry leaders warn the burgeoning, self-improving technology could spell doomsday for humanity if left unchecked.

The Democratic governor signed an executive order Tuesday establishing the Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet to assess “the various risks posed by Al to the safety of Illinois residents and the critical infrastructure residents rely on.”

Pritzker will name his AI Cabinet members “in the coming weeks” to work alongside numerous state agency leaders, including from the Department of Innovation and Technology, the Department of Public Health and the Illinois Emergency Management Agency.

They’re expected to come from backgrounds in academia, law, ethics and governance, and provide recommendations on potential public safety threats, protecting public assets and evaluating possible regulations, according to Pritzker’s office.

His order comes in the wake of former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s media blitz this month warning that aggressive industry development in the absence of federal regulation “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Meta chairman Mark Zuckerberg and other AI executives have emphasized the need for broader safety measures.

“Artificial Intelligence has enormous potential to transform our everyday lives, but when experts and industry leaders sound the alarm bell, urge us to slow down, and ask for guardrails, we should listen,” Pritzker said in a statement.
In July, Pritzker signed a package of state-level AI regulations into law that mark some of the most stringent in the nation, requiring frontier developers to submit to annual independent audits.
Pritzker, who has done little to quell speculation about his own presidential ambitions, has blasted President Donald Trump for his administration’s lax approach to AI regulation.

“Illinois has already enacted nation-leading laws that hold Big Tech accountable and today I’m taking executive action to keep this a priority,” Pritzker said. “Congress and the White House need to treat AI risks with urgency, but in the meantime, Illinois won’t wait because it is our foremost responsibility to prepare and protect Illinoisans.”

University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Chancellor Charles Isbell said in a statement that his institution is “eager to help the state navigate the current challenges and opportunities that AI brings.”

“As a land-grant institution, we are committed to innovation for the public good and to developing human-centered AI that protects privacy, reduces bias, strengthens democratic institutions, uses energy wisely, and creates value for workers, companies and communities,” Isbell said.

sources.title: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council - The Guardian
passages: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products.
Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade.
He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said.
“At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council.
“AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.
They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards.

Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.

“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.

The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry.

Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.

He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models.

While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.

AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk.

Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

Trump rejects international AI regulation, says United States will lead in safe, responsible manner. Whether to emphasise AI governance risks or UN event security . 9 of 11 outlets skipped it: deepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng does not plan to attend . NBC News was read line by line by the Watchdog : 6.1 . See the score → Al Jazeera foregrounds AI catastrophe warnings to urge global regulation. ABC7 emphasises UN summit security, traffic and counter-drone measures. World leaders called for stronger international safeguards and oversight on artificial intelligence during the general debate of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urging stronger global coordination to manage AI risks. Guterres warned, "The danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability," as U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI. French President Emmanuel Macron said, "We must build the capacity to audit these models rather than depend on a handful of private actors," while Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva criticized the concentration of technological power and warned of "a race with no ethical boundaries". South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said AI benefits could deepen inequality and imbalance "unless we are properly prepared for it," and he said South Korea would establish a global AI hub to tackle shared challenges ranging from climate change to health and food security. The debate was set to move from the General Assembly to the UN Security Council on Wednesday, when the council was scheduled to discuss AI and international security. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng does not plan to attend . Reported by 101 WIXX and BigGo Finance . Heads of major AI firms told the UN Security Council that the industry urgently needed global oversight, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warning, "If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world could "lose control of the future of AI," and he argued, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone." Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue told the council that his company had relied on a Chinese AI model to defend itself in incidents involving out-of-control AI models, saying, "We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI." The United States administration pushed back through its representative Michael Kratsios, who told members, "We totally reject all efforts by international bodies to assert centralised control and global governance of AI." Daniel Forti, head of UN Affairs at the International Crisis Group, said member states understood there would be a need for international cooperation and rules for AI even if the biggest players focused on growth opportunities. The UN debate centered on whether humans or machines should control life-and-death decisions, and it highlighted worries about AI use in warfare including machines making decisions without human control. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the Security Council that the tech leaders "are telling us in stark terms that it cannot be left to them to prevent disaster from befalling the world," and he added, "We cannot ignore them because they are right." Michael Kratsios pushed back again by saying control concerns were "not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structure," while he said, "We want you, our allies and partners, to share in the benefits of this technology." UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots," and Kentaro Toyama said, "Killer robots are technically easy to build, and they are real." The meeting also placed the issue in a wider diplomatic sequence, with the discussion unfolding as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit and as Trump was expected to meet Xi in Washington amid escalating competition between the two countries to develop and dominate the technology. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI , Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

extraction.body: UN Secretary-General calls for binding international safeguards and oversight on artificial intelligence. Trump rejects international AI regulation, says United States will lead in safe, responsible manner. Whether to emphasise AI governance risks or UN event security . 9 of 11 outlets skipped it: deepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng does not plan to attend . NBC News was read line by line by the Watchdog : 6.1 . See the score → Al Jazeera foregrounds AI catastrophe warnings to urge global regulation. ABC7 emphasises UN summit security, traffic and counter-drone measures. World leaders called for stronger international safeguards and oversight on artificial intelligence during the general debate of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urging stronger global coordination to manage AI risks. Guterres warned, "The danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability," as U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI. French President Emmanuel Macron said, "We must build the capacity to audit these models rather than depend on a handful of private actors," while Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva criticized the concentration of technological power and warned of "a race with no ethical boundaries". South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said AI benefits could deepen inequality and imbalance "unless we are properly prepared for it," and he said South Korea would establish a global AI hub to tackle shared challenges ranging from climate change to health and food security. The debate was set to move from the General Assembly to the UN Security Council on Wednesday, when the council was scheduled to discuss AI and international security. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng does not plan to attend . Reported by 101 WIXX and BigGo Finance . Heads of major AI firms told the UN Security Council that the industry urgently needed global oversight, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warning, "If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world could "lose control of the future of AI," and he argued, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone." Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue told the council that his company had relied on a Chinese AI model to defend itself in incidents involving out-of-control AI models, saying, "We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI." The United States administration pushed back through its representative Michael Kratsios, who told members, "We totally reject all efforts by international bodies to assert centralised control and global governance of AI." Daniel Forti, head of UN Affairs at the International Crisis Group, said member states understood there would be a need for international cooperation and rules for AI even if the biggest players focused on growth opportunities. The UN debate centered on whether humans or machines should control life-and-death decisions, and it highlighted worries about AI use in warfare including machines making decisions without human control. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the Security Council that the tech leaders "are telling us in stark terms that it cannot be left to them to prevent disaster from befalling the world," and he added, "We cannot ignore them because they are right." Michael Kratsios pushed back again by saying control concerns were "not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structure," while he said, "We want you, our allies and partners, to share in the benefits of this technology." UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots," and Kentaro Toyama said, "Killer robots are technically easy to build, and they are real." The meeting also placed the issue in a wider diplomatic sequence, with the discussion unfolding as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit and as Trump was expected to meet Xi in Washington amid escalating competition between the two countries to develop and dominate the technology. sources.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
passages: Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days.
Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks.
You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too.
Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent.

extraction.body: There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse, Meta's new AI agent. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps. One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks.
First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters).
I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it).
If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more?
School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible.
An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life.
But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use?

Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications.
Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest.
While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me.

But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue.
They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in.
The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out.
I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of.
I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data.
It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks).
I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November.
After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office.
The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone.
It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees.
A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance.
But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself.
Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet).
"Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me.
"If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through.
I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps.
One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks.
First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters).
I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it).
If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more?
School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible.
An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life.
But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use?

Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications.
Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest.
While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me.

But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue.
They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in.
The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out.
I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of.
I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data.
It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks).
I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November.
After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office.
The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone.
It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees.
A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance.
But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself.
Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet).
"Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me.
"If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through.
I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps.
One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do.

Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) opened at $86,195.28 on Wednesday, September 23, 2026 , flat compared to Tuesday's opening price. As of 7:26 a.m. ET this morning, the price of bitcoin moved lower to $85,600.03. Ethereum ( ETH-USD ) opened at $2,753.25 on Wednesday, September 23, 2026 , down 0.8% from Tuesday's opening price. The price of ethereum moved down this morning to $2,725.32 as of 7:26 a.m. ET. Back in 2024, BigBear.ai's quarterly sales towered over IONQ.
This makes sense given the former operates in the hot artificial intelligence sector while the latter focuses on nascent quantum computing technology.
Since then, a dramatic transformation has taken place.
This illustrates the potential for IONQ's business to soar once quantum machines achieve widespread adoption.

23, it announced a partnership with AI semiconductor leader Nvidia , where IONQ's latest quantum computer will connect with Nvidia's AI infrastructure to enable "large-scale quantum supercomputers capable of solving the world's hardest problems," according to IONQ.
